danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 22
paragraphs: Mens disse samtaler foregik i forværelset og i prinsessens værelse, rullede en vogn med Pierre (der var blevet sendt bud efter) og Anna Mikhajlovna (Boris' moder, som fandt det nødvendigt at ledsage ham) ind i gården til grev Bezukhovs palæ. Da hjulene blidt rullede hen over halmen, der var strøet under vinduerne, opdagede Anna Mikhajlovna, der lige havde trøstet sin rejsefælle med venlige ord, at han sad og sov i sit hjørne og vækkede ham. Pierre vågnede, fulgte Anna Mikhajlovna ud af vognen og begyndte først da at tænke på det møde med sin døende far, der ventede ham. Han bemærkede, at de ikke var kørt til hovedindgangen, men til bagdøren. Mens han steg ud af vogntrinnet, så han to mænd, der lignede handlende, løbe hastigt fra indgangen og gemme sig i husets skygge. Pierre lagde også mærke til adskillige andre mænd af samme slags, der skjulte sig i skyggen på begge sider af huset. Men hverken Anna Mikhajlovna eller lakajen eller kusken, der umuligt kunne undgå at se disse mennesker, tog notits af dem. »Det er nok i orden,« tænkte Pierre og fulgte Anna Mikhajlovna. Hun skyndte sig op ad den smalle, dunkelt oplyste stentrappe og kaldte på Pierre, der haltede bagefter, om at følge med. Selvom han ikke kunne se, hvorfor det var nødvendigt for ham overhovedet at besøge greven, endnu mindre hvorfor han skulle gå ad bagtrappen, så bedømte han ud fra Anna Mikhajlovnas beslutsomme og forjagede mine, at det hele var absolut nødvendigt. Halvvejs oppe ad trappen blev de næsten væltet af nogle mænd, der kom løbende ned med spande, mens deres støvler klaskede mod trinene. Disse mænd trykkede sig ind mod væggen for at lade Pierre og Anna Mikhajlovna passere og viste ikke den mindste overraskelse over at se dem dér.
»Er det her, man kommer til prinsessernes værelser?« spurgte Anna Mikhajlovna en af dem.
»Ja,« svarede en lakaj med dristig, høj røst, som om alt nu var tilladt, »døren til venstre, frue.«
»Måske har greven slet ikke bedt om mig,« sagde Pierre, da de nåede afsatsen. »Jeg burde hellere gå op på mit eget værelse.«
Anna Mikhajlovna standsede og ventede på, at han indhentede hende.
»Åh, min ven!« sagde hun og rørte hans arm, som hun havde gjort med sin søn om eftermiddagen, »tro mig, jeg lider ikke mindre end du, men vær en mand!«
»Men virkelig, var det ikke bedre, om jeg gik?« spurgte han og kiggede venligt på hende over sine briller.

»Åh, min kære ven! Glem de uretfærdigheder, du måtte have lidt. Tænk på, at han er din far ... måske i dødens kval.« Hun sukkede. »Jeg har elsket dig som en søn fra første færd. Stol på mig, Pierre. Jeg glemmer ikke dine interesser.«
Pierre forstod ikke et ord, men overbevisningen om, at alt dette var nødvendigt, voksede sig stærkere, og han fulgte lydigt Anna Mikhajlovna, der allerede var ved at åbne en dør.

Denne dør førte ind til et bagværelse. En gammel tjener, der hørte til prinsesserne, sad i et hjørne og strikkede en strømpe. Pierre havde aldrig været i denne del af huset og kendte ikke engang til disse værelsers eksistens. Anna Mikhajlovna tiltalte en stuepige, der skyndte sig forbi med en karaffel på et fad, som »min kære« og »min søde« og spurgte til prinsessens helbred. Derpå førte hun Pierre ned ad en stenkorridor. Den første dør til venstre førte ind til prinsessernes lejlighed. Stuepigen med karaflen havde i sin hast ikke lukket døren (alt i huset skete i hast på det tidspunkt), og Pierre og Anna Mikhajlovna kastede uvilkårligt et blik ind i rummet, da de passerede, hvor fyrst Vasilij og den ældste prinsesse sad tæt sammen og talte lavmælt. Da de så dem passere, trak fyrst Vasilij sig tilbage med tydelig utålmodighed, mens prinsessen sprang op og i en gestus af desperation smækkede døren i med al sin kraft.

Denne handling var så ulig hendes sædvanlige fatning, og den frygt, der afspejlede sig i fyrst Vasilijs ansigt, så uforenelig med hans værdighed, at Pierre standsede og så spørgende over sine briller på sin ledsager. Anna Mikhajlovna viste ingen overraskelse; hun smilede blot svagt og sukkede, som ville hun sige, at dette ikke var mere, end hun havde ventet.
»Vær en mand, min ven. Jeg passer på dine interesser,« sagde hun som svar på hans blik og gik endnu hurtigere ned ad korridoren.

Pierre forstod ikke, hvad det hele gik ud på, og endnu mindre hvad det betød at »passe på hans interesser«, men han besluttede, at alt dette måtte være nødvendigt. Fra korridoren gik de ind i et stort, dunkelt oplyst rum ved siden af grevens forværelse. Det var et af de luksuøse, men kolde rum, som Pierre kun kendte fra hoveddøren, men selv i dette rum stod der nu et tomt badekar, og der var spildt vand på tæppet. De blev mødt af en diakon med et røgelseskar og en tjener, der passerede dem på tåspidserne uden at ænse dem. De gik ind i det forværelse, som Pierre kendte, med to italienske vinduer ud mod vinterhaven, med sin store buste og sit portræt i fuld figur af Katarina den Store. De samme mennesker sad der stadig i næsten de samme positioner og hviskede til hinanden. Alle blev tavse og vendte sig for at se på den blege, forgrædte Anna Mikhajlovna, da hun trådte ind, og på den store, svære Pierre, der med bøjet hoved ydmygt fulgte efter hende.

Anna Mikhajlovnas ansigt udtrykte en bevidsthed om, at det afgørende øjeblik var kommet. Med minen af en erfaren petersborgsk dame trådte hun nu, med Pierre tæt ved sin side, ind i rummet med endnu større beslutsomhed end om eftermiddagen. Hun følte, at da hun bragte den person, den døende ønskede at se, var hendes egen adgang sikret. Med et hurtigt blik på alle i rummet og med øje for grevens skriftefader gled hun hen til ham i en slags trippende gang, ikke ligefrem neiende, men som om hun pludseligt blev mindre, og modtog ærbødigt velsignelsen, først fra den ene, så fra den anden præst.

»Gud være lovet, at De kom i tide,« sagde hun til en af præsterne; »vi pårørende har været i en sådan ængstelse. Denne unge mand er grevens søn,« tilføjede hun mere dæmpet. »Hvilket forfærdeligt øjeblik!«
Med de ord gik hun hen til lægen.
»Kære doktor,« sagde hun, »denne unge mand er grevens søn. Er der noget håb?«

Lægen kastede et hurtigt blik opad og trak tavst på skuldrene. Anna Mikhajlovna hævede med nøjagtig den samme bevægelse sine skuldre og øjne, næsten lukkede dem, sukkede og bevægede sig væk fra lægen hen til Pierre. Til ham sagde hun i en særligt ærbødig og ømt bedrøvet stemme:
»Stol på Hans nåde!« Og idet hun pegede på en lille sofa, hvor han kunne sidde og vente, gled hun lydløst hen mod den dør, som alle iagttog, og den knirkede ganske svagt, da hun forsvandt bag den.

Pierre, der havde besluttet sig for blindt at adlyde sin vejlederinde, gik hen mod den sofa, hun havde anvist. Straks Anna Mikhajlovna var forsvundet, bemærkede han, at alles øjne i rummet rettede sig mod ham med noget mere end nysgerrighed og medfølelse. Han lagde mærke til, at de hviskede til hinanden og kastede betydningsfulde blikke i hans retning med en slags ærefrygt og endda underdanighed. Man viste ham en agtelse, som han aldrig før havde oplevet. En fremmed dame, hende der havde talt med præsterne, rejste sig og tilbød ham sin plads; en adjudant samlede en handske op, Pierre havde tabt, og rakte ham den; lægerne blev ærbødigt tavse, da han gik forbi, og rykkede til side for ham. Pierre ville først tage en anden plads for ikke at genere damen og ville selv samle handsken op og gå uden om lægerne, der slet ikke stod i vejen for ham; men han følte pludselig, at det ikke gik an, og at han denne aften var en person, der var forpligtet til at udføre en slags forfærdelig ceremoni, som alle forventede af ham, og at han derfor måtte acceptere deres tjenester. Han tog handsken tavst fra adjudanten, satte sig i damens stol, lagde sine store hænder symmetrisk på sine knæ i den naive positur af en ægyptisk statue og besluttede for sig selv, at alt var, som det skulle være, og at han for ikke at miste fatningen og gøre dumme ting i aften ikke måtte handle på egne tanker, men helt overgive sig til dem, der ledte ham.

Der gik ikke to minutter, før fyrst Vasilij med løftet hoved majestætisk trådte ind i rummet. Han var iført sin lange frakke med tre stjerner på brystet. Han virkede tyndere end om morgenen; hans øjne syntes større end sædvanligt, da han så sig om og opdagede Pierre. Han gik hen til ham, tog hans hånd (noget han aldrig plejede at gøre) og trak den nedad, som om han ville sikre sig, at den sad godt fast.
»Mod, mod, min ven! Han har bedt om at se dig. Det er godt!« og han vendte sig for at gå.
Men Pierre fandt det nødvendigt at spørge: »Hvordan har...« og tøvede, usikker på om det ville være passende at kalde den døende »greven«, men skammede sig over at kalde ham »far«.
»Han fik endnu et slagtilfælde for en halv time siden. Mod, min ven...«

Pierres tanker var i en sådan forvirring, at ordet »slagtilfælde« fik ham til at tænke på et slag fra noget. Han så forvirret på fyrst Vasilij og forstod først senere, at et slagtilfælde var et anfald af sygdom. Fyrst Vasilij sagde noget til Lorrain i forbifarten og gik på tåspidserne hen mod døren. Han kunne ikke gå godt på tåspidserne, og hele hans krop rykkede ved hvert skridt. Den ældste prinsesse fulgte efter ham, og præster, diakoner og nogle tjenere gik også ind ad døren. Gennem den dør hørtes en lyd af ting, der blev rykket rundt, og endelig kom Anna Mikhajlovna, stadig med det samme udtryk, bleg men beslutsom i udførelsen af sin pligt, løbende ud og rørte let Pierres arm og sagde:
»Den guddommelige barmhjertighed er uudtømmelig! Den sidste olie skal gives. Kom.«

Pierre gik ind ad døren, trådte på det bløde tæppe og lagde mærke til, at den fremmede dame, adjudanten og nogle af tjenerne alle fulgte efter ham, som om der nu ikke længere var brug for tilladelse til at gå ind i det rum.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: While these conversations were taking place in the reception room and the princess's room, a carriage carrying Pierre—who had been sent for—and Anna Mikhaylovna, who felt it necessary to accompany him, was pulling into the courtyard of Count Bezukhov's house. As the wheels rolled softly over the straw that had been laid beneath the windows, Anna Mikhaylovna turned to offer some comforting words to her companion—and realized he was asleep in his corner. She woke him up. Pierre roused himself and followed Anna Mikhaylovna out of the carriage, only then beginning to think about the visit with his dying father that lay ahead. He noticed they hadn't come to the front entrance but to a back door. As he was climbing down from the carriage, two men who looked like tradesmen darted away from the entrance and hid in the shadows along the wall. Pausing, Pierre spotted several other men of the same type lurking in the shadows on both sides of the house. But neither Anna Mikhaylovna nor the footman nor the coachman—who couldn't have missed seeing them—paid any attention. "It must be all right," Pierre told himself, and followed Anna Mikhaylovna. She hurried up a narrow, dimly lit stone staircase, calling back to Pierre, who was falling behind, to keep up. Though he couldn't see why it was necessary for him to visit the count at all, much less why they had to use the back stairs, Anna Mikhaylovna's air of confidence and urgency made Pierre conclude that it was all absolutely essential. Halfway up, they were nearly knocked over by some men carrying pails who came clattering down the stairs in heavy boots. These men pressed themselves against the wall to let Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna pass, showing not the slightest surprise at seeing them there.
"Is this the way to the princesses' apartments?" Anna Mikhaylovna asked one of them.
"Yes," a footman answered in a bold, loud voice, as though anything were now permissible. "The door on the left, ma'am."
"Perhaps the count didn't ask for me," Pierre said when they reached the landing. "I'd better go to my own room."
Anna Mikhaylovna stopped and waited for him to catch up.
"Oh, my friend!" she said, touching his arm just as she had touched her son's that afternoon. "Believe me, I'm suffering no less than you are, but be a man!"
"But really, shouldn't I just go?" he asked, looking at her kindly over his spectacles.

"Oh, my dear friend! Forget whatever wrongs may have been done to you. Remember—he is your father... perhaps in the agony of death." She sighed. "I've loved you like a son from the very beginning. Trust me, Pierre. I won't forget your interests."
Pierre didn't understand a word of this, but his growing conviction that all of it was necessary only strengthened, and he meekly followed Anna Mikhaylovna, who was already opening a door.

The door led into a back anteroom. In one corner, an old servant of the princesses sat knitting a stocking. Pierre had never been in this part of the house and didn't even know these rooms existed. Anna Mikhaylovna addressed a maid hurrying past with a decanter on a tray as "my dear" and "my sweet," asked about the princess's health, and then led Pierre down a stone passage. The first door on the left opened into the princesses' apartments. The maid with the decanter, in her haste, had left the door open—everything in the house was being done in haste just then—and as Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna passed, they instinctively glanced inside. There sat Prince Vasili and the eldest princess, close together, talking intensely. Seeing them pass, Prince Vasili drew back with obvious irritation, while the princess leaped up and, in a gesture of desperation, slammed the door shut with all her strength.

This was so unlike the princess's usual composure, and the fear on Prince Vasili's face so out of keeping with his dignity, that Pierre stopped and looked questioningly over his spectacles at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna showed no surprise. She only gave a faint smile and sighed, as if to say this was no more than she had expected.
"Be a man, my friend. I'll look after your interests," she said in response to his look, and walked even faster down the corridor.

Pierre couldn't make sense of any of it, least of all what "looking after his interests" meant, but he decided that all these things simply had to happen. From the corridor they entered a large, dimly lit room next to the count's reception room. It was one of those grand but cold apartments Pierre knew only from approaching through the front entrance, but now even this room had an empty bathtub standing in it, and water had been spilled on the carpet. A deacon with a censer and a servant passed them on tiptoe without so much as a glance. They continued into the reception room that Pierre knew well, with its two Italian windows facing the conservatory, its large bust, and its full-length portrait of Catherine the Great. The same people sat there in nearly the same positions as before, whispering among themselves. They all fell silent and turned to look at Anna Mikhaylovna—pale and tear-stained—as she entered, and at Pierre's large, heavy figure following meekly behind her with his head bowed.

Anna Mikhaylovna's expression conveyed her awareness that the decisive moment had arrived. With the manner of a practical Petersburg lady, she entered the room even more boldly than she had that afternoon, keeping Pierre close beside her. She knew that by bringing the person the dying man had asked to see, her own presence was assured. Scanning the room with a quick glance and noticing the count's confessor, she glided over to him in a kind of half-bow—seeming to grow suddenly smaller—and respectfully received the blessing first of one priest, then another.
"Thank God you've come in time," she said to one of the priests. "We relatives have all been so worried. This young man is the count's son," she added more softly. "What a terrible moment!"
Then she went up to the doctor.
"Dear doctor," she said, "this young man is the count's son. Is there any hope?"

The doctor glanced upward quickly and gave a silent shrug. Anna Mikhaylovna mirrored the exact same movement—raising her shoulders and eyes, nearly closing them—sighed, and turned away from the doctor to Pierre. In a particularly respectful and tenderly sorrowful voice, she said:
"Trust in His mercy!" Then, pointing him to a small sofa where he could sit and wait, she moved silently toward the door everyone was watching. It gave a faint creak as she disappeared behind it.

Pierre, having resolved to obey his guide in everything, moved toward the sofa she had indicated. The moment Anna Mikhaylovna vanished, he noticed that every pair of eyes in the room was fixed on him with something more than curiosity and sympathy. People whispered to one another, casting meaningful glances his way with a kind of awe—even deference. He had never been treated like this before. A strange lady, the one who had been talking with the priests, stood up and offered him her seat. An aide-de-camp picked up a glove Pierre had dropped and returned it to him. The doctors fell respectfully silent as he passed and moved aside for him. At first Pierre wanted to take a different seat so as not to inconvenience the lady, and to pick up the glove himself, and to walk around the doctors who weren't even in his way. But all at once he sensed that this wouldn't do—that tonight he was a person expected to perform some kind of solemn ritual, and therefore obliged to accept their attentions. He took the glove from the aide-de-camp in silence, sat down in the lady's chair, and placed his large hands symmetrically on his knees in the naive pose of an Egyptian statue. He had decided that in order not to lose his head and do something foolish, he must not act on his own judgment tonight but surrender himself entirely to the will of those guiding him.

Less than two minutes later, Prince Vasili entered the room with his head held high, looking majestic. He wore his long coat with three stars on his chest. He seemed even thinner than he had that morning; his eyes appeared larger than usual as he surveyed the room and spotted Pierre. He walked over, took Pierre's hand—something he had never done before—and pulled it downward, as if testing whether it was firmly attached.
"Courage, courage, my friend! He's asked to see you. That's good!" And he turned to go.
But Pierre felt he should ask: "How is..." He hesitated, unsure whether it was proper to call the dying man "the count," yet embarrassed to call him "father."
"He had another stroke about half an hour ago. Courage, my friend..."

Pierre's mind was in such a fog that the word "stroke" made him think of a physical blow. He stared at Prince Vasili in confusion, and only later grasped that a stroke meant an attack of illness. Prince Vasili murmured something to Lorrain in passing and went through the door on tiptoe. He wasn't good at walking on tiptoe, and his whole body lurched with each step. The eldest princess followed him, and the priests, deacons, and some servants also went through the door. Behind it came the sound of things being moved around, and finally Anna Mikhaylovna—still wearing the same expression, pale but resolute in the performance of duty—hurried out, lightly touched Pierre's arm, and said:
"God's mercy is boundless! They are about to administer last rites. Come."

Pierre went through the door, stepping onto the soft carpet, and noticed that the strange lady, the aide-de-camp, and several servants all followed him in, as though there were no longer any need for permission to enter that room.
